segments.original: In the wake of the 2001 terrorist attacks, there were visible signs of soul-searching in American cinema. Spike Lee (b. 1957) responded with the heartfelt 25th Hour (2002). The film, which revolves around the last day of freedom of a man about to be sent to prison, is a love letter to Lee's beloved New York as well as a study of consequences and responsibility.

segments.original: Dramatized reconstructions of what happened on September 11 were dominated by Paul Greengrass's (b. 1955) harrowing United 93 (2006). Oliver Stone's (b. 1946) World Trade Center (2006) drew criticism from all sides. Stone was also criticized for his biopic of George W. Bush, W. (2008). Although it was far from the devastating indictment some had hoped for, Stone's aim was to pose a more ambitious challenge to a system that allowed a man like him to reach the Oval Office.

segments.original: The Oscar-winning The Hurt Locker (2008) could be read as an endorsement of either left- or right-wing positions on the conflict in Iraq. segments.original: In the aftermath of 9/11, filmmakers found themselves looking to the past, to American history, and to the roots of the national psyche. Paul Thomas Anderson (b. 1970) directed There Will Be Blood (2007) and conveyed the message that many contemporary films explored during the Bush administration - that power corrupts and breeds paranoia and fear in those who benefit from it. With Gangs of New York (2002) and The Aviator (2004), Martin Scorsese (b. 1942) examined the birth of the modern United States - capitalism, racial tensions, and, in the characters of the brutal Bill the Butcher and the unstable millionaire Howard Hughes, the dangers of greed and isolationism.
